title: Kierkegaard and the Birth of Existentialism
description: The single individual, anxiety, and the leap of faith

concepts.title: Against the System
concepts.contentHtml:
Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) launched his life's work as a sustained polemic against Hegel. Hegel's system, he argued, may comprehend everything in thought but leaves out the one thing that matters most: the existing individual.

'An existential system is impossible.' Existence is something a person is, not something that can be summarised in a category. Pure thought operates in a timeless logical present; a real human being is a concrete, decisive, suffering self living in time, facing death.

The watchword 'truth is subjectivity' does not mean truth is whatever you feel; it means that the truths that matter most — about how to live — must be appropriated by the individual in inwardness, not contemplated from a distance.

concepts.title: The Three Stages on Life's Way
concepts.contentHtml:
Kierkegaard sketches three modes of existence:

Aesthetic: life lived for novelty, pleasure, immediacy. The aesthete (figured by Don Juan or 'the seducer') flits from one experience to another and finally collapses into despair when external stimulation can no longer cover the void.

Ethical: life lived as commitment — marriage, work, civic duty. The ethical individual chooses themself, takes on the universal moral order, and finds stability through resolve.

Religious: life lived in relation to the absolute. Here the individual confronts what the ethical cannot reach: their own absolute responsibility before God, sin, and grace.

Each stage is reached by a leap, not by argument. There is no smooth dialectical ascent.

concepts.title: Anxiety and the Leap of Faith
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Concept of Anxiety (1844) Kierkegaard treats anxiety (Angst) not as a malfunction but as the dizziness of freedom. Faced with possibility — with the fact that I could be otherwise — finite consciousness reels.

Fear and Trembling dramatises Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac as the teleological suspension of the ethical. Abraham's act, judged by ordinary morality, is murder. Yet his obedience to God involves a relation to the absolute that ethics cannot evaluate. To believe is to act in the face of the absurd, with no rational guarantee.

Faith, for Kierkegaard, is not certainty but a leap: the existing individual stakes everything on what reason cannot demonstrate. This existential structure — anxiety, decision, the absurd — is the seedbed of twentieth-century existentialism.

title: Nietzsche: Death of God and Will to Power
description: Genealogy of morals, eternal recurrence, and the Übermensch

concepts.title: The Death of God
concepts.contentHtml:
Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) announced in The Gay Science that 'God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.' This is a cultural diagnosis, not a metaphysical thesis: belief in the Christian-Platonic God has lost its grip on European consciousness, and with it the entire framework of values that depended on it.

The danger Nietzsche names is nihilism — the long shadow cast by God's death, when the highest values devalue themselves and 'the why finds no answer.' If God dies but we keep his moral table of values, we live in incoherent piety.

The task of philosophy after God is therefore the revaluation of all values: not nostalgic restoration, not despairing nihilism, but the creation of new values from the standpoint of life itself.

concepts.title: Genealogy and Will to Power
concepts.contentHtml:
In On the Genealogy of Morals (1887) Nietzsche traces the history of moral concepts. Originally 'good' meant noble, strong, life-affirming; 'bad' meant base, weak. The slave revolt in morality reversed this: the powerless redescribed their weakness as virtue and their oppressors' strength as evil. Pity, humility, meekness become 'good'; pride, vitality, self-assertion become 'evil'.

Ressentiment — the impotent rage of the weak — is the engine. Christian morality is, for Nietzsche, the most successful slave morality, fortified by the ascetic priest who turns suffering into meaning by blaming the sufferer.

The deeper drive Nietzsche calls will to power: not domination but the basic dynamic of all becoming — every drive, every life-form striving to extend, organise, and overcome itself.

concepts.title: Eternal Recurrence and the Übermensch
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Gay Science (§341), and then at the heart of Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Nietzsche presents the eternal recurrence of the same as 'the heaviest weight'. Imagine a demon whispering: this life as you now live it you will have to live again, infinitely many times, with every pain and joy in identical sequence. Would you crush him, or call him a god?

The recurrence is less a cosmological claim than an existential test. Only one who has so wholly affirmed life — every detail, every wound — that they would will it eternally has achieved amor fati: love of fate.

The Übermensch ('overhuman') is the one capable of this affirmation: who creates values rather than receives them, who has no need of metaphysical comfort, who treats life as something to be made into an artwork. Not a fascist superman — Nietzsche despised German nationalism and antisemitism — but a regulative ideal of self-overcoming.

concepts.title: The Question of Being and Dasein
concepts.contentHtml:
Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) opens Being and Time (1927) by reviving the oldest philosophical question: what does it mean for anything to be? Western metaphysics, he claims, has forgotten the ontological difference between beings (entities) and Being (the fact that they are at all).

To re-pose the question we need a starting point — an entity for whom Being is itself an issue. Heidegger names this entity Dasein (literally 'being-there'): you and I, in our concrete existence. Dasein is not a thing among things; it is a kind of being whose own being is at stake.

The structure Heidegger uncovers is being-in-the-world: not a subject staring at an object, but a unified involvement with a meaningful environment. We always already understand the world before any theoretical reflection.

concepts.title: Ready-to-Hand and the Breakdown
concepts.contentHtml:
Heidegger argues that our primary mode of encountering things is not detached observation but concernful coping. A hammer is not first a chunk of wood and metal we then judge to be useful; it is, in its hammering, ready-to-hand (zuhanden). It withdraws into the activity it makes possible.

Only when the hammer breaks, is missing, or stands in the way does it become present-at-hand (vorhanden) — a mere object with properties. This breakdown phenomenon, for Heidegger, reveals the prior structure of equipment, references, and assignments that made smooth use possible.

The implication is far-reaching: traditional philosophy started from the present-at-hand (atoms, substances) and asked how mind reaches out to them. Heidegger reverses the order — the theoretical attitude is a derivative mode of a more basic engaged understanding.

concepts.title: Anxiety, Authenticity, and Being-Toward-Death
concepts.contentHtml:
Most of the time Dasein lives as das Man ('the They') — doing what one does, saying what one says, fleeing the burden of being a self.

Anxiety (Angst) is the mood that breaks this absorption. Unlike fear (which has a definite object), anxiety has no object: the world as a whole becomes uncanny, recedes into insignificance. In anxiety, Dasein faces its own naked thrownness and finitude.

Being-toward-death is the formal structure that anxiety reveals. Death is not an event at the end of my life but a possibility that runs through every moment as the possibility of having no further possibilities. To own this possibility — rather than evade it through everyday distraction — is to live authentically: as a finite, individual self that takes responsibility for its own existence.

title: Sartre: Freedom and Bad Faith
description: Existence precedes essence, the look, and radical responsibility

concepts.title: Existence Precedes Essence
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) crystallised existentialism in his 1945 lecture Existentialism is a Humanism with the slogan: existence precedes essence.

For a manufactured object — a paper-knife — the essence (the design, the purpose) precedes its existence; we make it because we know what it is for. Traditional theology treated humans this way, with God as the artisan. Strip away God and the formula reverses for human beings: we exist first, encounter ourselves in the world, and then define ourselves by our choices.

There is no human nature waiting to be discovered. 'Man is nothing else but what he makes of himself.' This is at once a description and a charter of responsibility.

concepts.title: Being-In-Itself, Being-For-Itself, Bad Faith
concepts.contentHtml:
Being and Nothingness (1943) distinguishes two modes of being. Being-in-itself (en-soi) is the dense, self-identical being of things — a stone simply is what it is. Being-for-itself (pour-soi) is consciousness, which is precisely not what it is and is what it is not: a perpetual transcendence of any given state toward future possibilities.

Because consciousness is freedom — a 'nothingness' separating it from all factual being — we are 'condemned to be free'. We cannot not choose; even refusal is choice.

This is unbearable, so we lie to ourselves. Bad faith (mauvaise foi) is the attempt to flee freedom by pretending to be a thing. The waiter who plays at being-a-waiter, the lover who treats their feelings as fixed facts, anyone who says 'that's just how I am' — all evade the responsibility their freedom imposes.

concepts.title: The Look and the Other
concepts.contentHtml:
Sartre's analysis of intersubjectivity is dramatised by the look. Spying through a keyhole, I am pure consciousness aimed at the scene inside — until footsteps in the hall freeze me. Suddenly I am an object in someone else's world, judged, fixed, ashamed.

The Other's gaze constitutes me as a being I cannot wholly comprehend from inside my own freedom. This generates the dramatic conflicts of No Exit: 'Hell is other people' — not because others are evil, but because each consciousness inevitably objectifies the others.

For Sartre this conflict is structural. Yet his later work, including the unfinished Critique of Dialectical Reason (1960), tried to think genuine solidarity — the 'group-in-fusion' — without dissolving freedom. The political stake was Marxism after Stalinism: a humanism that takes both freedom and history seriously.

title: Camus and Beauvoir
description: The absurd, revolt, ambiguity, and the situation of woman

concepts.title: Camus and the Absurd
concepts.contentHtml:
Albert Camus (1913–1960) opens The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) with the claim that 'there is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' If life has no inherent meaning, why live?

The absurd, for Camus, is not a property of the world or of consciousness alone but of their encounter: a mind demanding meaning meeting a universe that refuses to provide it. The absurd cannot be dissolved by suicide (which abolishes one term of the encounter) or by what Camus calls philosophical suicide — the leap to faith or metaphysics that pretends meaning is given.

Sisyphus, condemned to roll his boulder eternally, is Camus's hero precisely because in the conscious moment of descent he embraces his fate. 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Revolt, lucidity, and joy without metaphysical guarantee.

concepts.title: Revolt and the Plague
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Rebel (1951) Camus extends the analysis from individual confrontation to collective politics. The rebel is the one who says 'No' — refusing humiliation — and in doing so affirms a value present in everyone. Genuine revolt has limits: it negates the dehumanising condition while affirming a shared humanity.

Revolutionary terror, for Camus, is rebellion gone mad: it sacrifices present persons for an abstract future, treating means as disposable. This argument famously fractured his friendship with Sartre, who defended a more dialectical relation to revolutionary violence.

The novel The Plague (1947) gives the doctrine narrative form. In a city under siege from disease, ordinary people choose decency without metaphysical reward — fighting an enemy they cannot defeat, because that is what being human in the absurd condition demands.

concepts.title: Beauvoir: Ambiguity and the Second Sex
concepts.contentHtml:
Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) developed an existential ethics in The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947). Sartre had described freedom as ontological. Beauvoir asked: how does freedom become a project — and what do we owe to the freedom of others?

Her answer: freedom is realised only by working to free others. Oppression is not merely an external constraint; it actively narrows the field of possibilities through which a self can become.

The masterpiece The Second Sex (1949) opens its second volume with a famous claim: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Womanhood is not a biological essence but a situation imposed on female humans by a culture that constitutes Man as the norm and Woman as the Other. Through phenomenological description of childhood, marriage, motherhood, and aging, Beauvoir shows how immanence (passivity, embeddedness in given roles) is enforced where transcendence (free project) ought to be possible. Existentialism here becomes a theory of liberation.
